title: A Future with Windows
subtitle: Stars Between the Strings · Chapter 38 of 40
content:
The new windows changed the room.

Not magically. They let morning sunlight reach the far wall, where paint had faded behind an old poster. Dust floated through the bright strip of air, and a plant Greg insisted was "pretty much immortal" looked alarmingly alive for the first time in weeks.

"See?" he said. "A whole different future."

"The future needs watering."

"That too."

We had repaired the small room where Greg practiced near Starwake Pier. It wasn't a grand house or an exclusive promise. It was a place he could use freely and I could visit when I chose, with windows that no longer rattled in every storm.

The repairs had taken twice as long as expected. Our first measurements were wrong. The replacement frame arrived with a cracked pane. Tamsin supervised the final fitting, and Greg paid the invoice instead of offering to play three free concerts in exchange for someone else's labor.

We stood inside with a pencil, a notebook, and a half-eaten bag of crackers.

"What goes where?" Greg asked.

"Music stand."

"Obviously."

"Chair near the window."

"Good."

"One shelf that isn't filled entirely with cables."

He looked wounded.

"You're asking me to give up my heritage."

"Your heritage includes seventeen identical adapters."

"Some of them are slightly different."

I laughed and took the pencil.

Greg drew a floor plan on the back of a grocery list. The room looked enormous in his sketch.

"That couch won't fit through the door."

"Sure it will."

"By bending space?"

He checked the doorway, then crossed out the couch.

"Fine. A heroic folding chair."

We measured the walls properly. I wrote down the numbers while Greg double-checked them. We both remembered the first window frame.

Then he found a picture of a wooden window seat and held it up like a proposal.

"Would you want one of these?"

"Maybe. But how much does it cost? Would it block the door? Could someone still reach the window latch?"

He studied the plan.

"You're right."

"And I don't want the room to become proof that I'm supposed to stay here forever."

His hand stopped.

"I didn't mean it that way."

"I know. That's why I'm telling you before we build something we can't undo."

He sat on the ledge, careful not to lean against the fresh frame.

"Sometimes I imagine your books and my guitar and enough space for Steven to visit," he said. "Then I remember you have other people you love, other places to go, and I start worrying I'm planning a house nobody has agreed to live in."

I sat beside him.

"You can imagine a future with me."

"Even if it isn't your only future?"

"Yes. I'm ethically non-monogamous and I prefer polyamory. That doesn't mean I can't want a room here too. It means we need to talk about what the room represents."

He looked out the window.

"So what does it represent?"

"A place you can call yours. A place where I can be welcome without being obligated to stay. A place where the people you love can visit by invitation, not assumption."

He smiled.

"I like that."

"And if I want a door I can close?"

"Then you close it. So do I."

"Radical home design."

We laughed.

At the hardware shop, the clerk showed us a folding chair that fit, a low shelf, and wall hooks rated for the guitar case. Greg wanted a bright purple curtain.

"Absolutely not."

"You're stifling my artistic expression."

"Your artistic expression can have a sample swatch before it becomes our problem."

We took the swatches.

Back at the room, Steven arrived with a potted plant.

"Thought the windows could use something green," he said.

Greg stared.

"Is that a cactus?"

"It's easy to care for."

"The last one died."

Steven looked at me.

"He overwatered it."

"That tracks."

Greg protested while we set the pot where it would get light without blocking the latch. Steven asked whether he could come by to record a song with his dad. Greg said yes, then checked the schedule instead of promising every day of the week.

I watched them make the plan.

This was what I wanted: a room that could hold different kinds of love without demanding they all became the same thing.

We wrote the folding chair into the room's inventory, along with the microphone stand and the little table that kept wobbling. Nola had asked for a list of everything stored there so volunteers could tell what belonged to the pier and what Greg had brought from Beach City.

"That seems like a lot of paperwork for one sad chair," Greg said.

"It's a very important sad chair."

He tried sitting in it. One leg bent, and we both froze.

"Okay. Less important than I thought."

We marked it for repair instead of pretending it would hold another visitor. Steven came back to check whether the cactus needed more light and found his father on the floor, testing chair legs.

"Everything okay?" he asked.

"Your dad's planning an exciting career in furniture design."

Steven laughed. He asked whether he could bring a friend to record later in the week. Greg looked at the schedule, confirmed the room would be free, and gave him Nola's contact for the actual equipment rules.

After Steven left, Greg stood by the new window.

"I used to picture the perfect place," he said. "Somewhere every song sounded great and nobody had to leave."

"And now?"

"Now I'd settle for a room people can come back to, even if the curtains are ugly."

I took his hand. There was an ache in his voice, but also a little hope. I had told him openly that I preferred polyamory and ethical non-monogamy. I didn't want to promise one shared future that left no room for the other people and places we loved.

"I like this room," I said. "And I like that you asked me before deciding what we would make of it."

He smiled. "Even with the chair?"

"Especially with the chair. It proves we still need a budget."

He kissed me after asking, and we laughed when the repaired window creaked in the wind. It was a real room, not a dream of perfect belonging, and I found it much easier to love for that.

After Steven left, we reviewed the window seat. The budget was tight after the repairs, and the folding chair would do for now. We drew a dotted outline on the plan, with a note to reconsider it after the next maintenance fund review.

Greg leaned on the doorframe.

"Do you think we're being too practical?"

"What would too practical look like?"

"Maybe a rule about how many times I can tell you I love you before the room gets boring."

I looked at him.

"That's not a practical problem."

"Just a thought."

I went to him and took his hand.

"You can tell me. I'm not going to measure it against the things I feel for other people."

He smiled.

"Good."

He kissed my forehead. We stayed there for a moment while the sea wind moved through the open window.

Then the curtain sample blew off the sill.

Greg lunged for it, tripped over the folding chair, and landed safely against the wall with an expression of wounded dignity.

"Majestic," I said.

"Exactly as planned."

We laughed until we had to sit down.

Before dusk we checked the exit was clear, the window latch worked, and the plant wasn't where the next storm would throw it onto the floor. Greg surveyed the room.

"Not much furniture."

"Enough."

"Plenty of future, though."

"You're starting to sound like a greeting card."

He laughed.

I sat in the heroic folding chair. Greg perched on the shelf until I reminded him it wasn't a bench. He settled on the floor beside me.

"Comfortable?" he asked.

"Yes."

"Can I kiss you?"

"Please."

He kissed me warmly, one hand resting against mine.

"Do you think this counts as building something together?" he asked.

"Even without the window seat?"

"Especially without it."

We turned down the lights and left the room tidy enough to use tomorrow. The rest of the evening stayed private, full of awkward kisses, laughter, and the freedom to fall asleep without performing a perfect future.

The next morning, the plant had survived.

The curtains remained undecided.

The future was not finished.

But the window opened smoothly, the door could close, and the people who loved this room were free to choose when to return.
